title: The Blue Planet We Named After Dirt
blurb: The only world we know with liquid water and life, spinning at a thousand miles an hour without you feeling a thing.

blocks.prompt: Read this out loud
blocks.text: This is Earth. Earth is the planet we live on. Earth is round like a big ball. The blue parts are water. The green parts are land. The white parts are clouds. You live on the land. blocks.prompt: The Ball You Are Standing On
blocks.text: Earth is a huge ball of rock, and you are standing on it right now. Earth spins. It turns all the way around one time every day. When your side faces the sun, you get daytime. When your side turns away, you get night. You cannot feel the spin. Everything spins with you. Your house spins. Your dog spins. The air spins. Even the clouds spin. Earth also has a moon. The moon goes around Earth again and again. Most of Earth is covered in water. That is why it looks blue from space.

daytime
one
because most of it is covered in water

blocks.prompt: The Water Planet With the Wrong Name
blocks.text: From space, Earth looks blue. There is a good reason for that. Water covers almost three quarters of the planet. Only about one quarter is land, and that small part is where every city, every forest, and every person sits. The oceans are deep, too. In some places the water goes down almost seven miles. Here is something strange. We named our planet Earth, and the old word earth means soil, or ground, or dirt. Every other planet in our solar system is named after an ancient god. Mars was a god of war. Jupiter was the king of the gods. Our planet ended up named after the stuff under our feet, even though most of it is ocean. Earth is also the only planet we know of where water stays liquid on the surface. It is not frozen solid. It is not boiled away into steam. It sits there, wet, for billions of years. That one fact may be the reason Earth is the only place we have ever found life.

answers: almost three quarters of it
soil, or ground, or dirt
every other planet is named after an ancient god
(inference: living things need water they can drink and live in, not ice or steam)

4.title: The Blue Planet We Named After Dirt
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

meta.templateLabel: The Blue Planet We Named After Dirt

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Spins about 1,000 mph at the equator
Orbits the sun at about 67,000 mph
Tilted over by 23.4 degrees
One trip around the sun takes 365 days
Sunlight reaches us in about 8 minutes

blocks.prompt: Sitting Still at a Thousand Miles an Hour
blocks.text: Right now you are sitting still. You are also moving faster than a jet plane. Both of those things are true at the same time. Earth spins once about every 24 hours. If you stand near the equator, that spin is carrying you east at roughly 1,000 miles per hour. At the same time, the whole planet is racing around the sun at about 67,000 miles per hour. You feel none of it. The reason is that everything around you is moving too. The ground, the air, your chair, your glass of water, all of it travels at the same speed in the same direction. You only feel motion when your speed or your direction changes. A car ride is boring in a straight line and exciting on a sharp corner. Earth's spin is smooth and steady, so it feels like nothing at all. The spin does one important job. It gives us day and night. But it is Earth's tilt, not its spin, that gives us the seasons. Earth leans over by about 23 degrees, and it keeps leaning the same way all year. For half the year your part of the planet leans toward the sun, so the light arrives strong and straight down and the days run long. For the other half it leans away, and the same sunlight arrives slanted, spread thin across more ground. That lean is the whole reason for summer and winter. It has nothing to do with being closer to the sun.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in full sentences.
items: The passage says you are sitting still and also moving faster than a jet plane. Explain how both can be true.
Why can you feel a car take a sharp corner but not feel Earth spinning?
A friend says summer happens because Earth moves closer to the sun. Use the passage to explain why that is wrong.
A person standing near the North Pole is carried east much more slowly than a person at the equator. Why do you think that is?
answers: you are still compared to the ground, but the ground itself is moving fast
the corner changes your direction; Earth's spin is smooth and steady so nothing changes
seasons come from Earth's tilt, not from distance to the sun
(inference: the pole travels a much smaller circle in the same 24 hours)

blocks.prompt: Circle the main idea of this passage.

The sun travels around Earth once every 24 hours
answers: Earth's steady spin and its tilt explain day, night, and the seasons, even though we never feel the motion

meta.templateLabel: The Blue Planet We Named After Dirt

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: About 4.5 billion years old
Air: 78 percent nitrogen, 21 percent oxygen
The Great Oxidation Event: 2.4 billion years ago
Outer core: liquid iron, 1,800 miles down
The magnetic field makes the aurora
Mars lost its field, then lost its air

blocks.prompt: The Planet That Built Its Own Sky
blocks.text: Take a breath. About one fifth of what just entered your lungs is oxygen, and none of it was here when the planet formed. Earth is roughly 4.5 billion years old. For the first two billion of those years, the air was mostly nitrogen and carbon dioxide, with almost no free oxygen at all. Any animal alive today would have suffocated in minutes. Then something very small changed everything. Tiny ocean bacteria, called cyanobacteria, worked out how to use sunlight to split water apart and build sugar out of the pieces. Oxygen was the leftover, the waste product they had no use for, and they poured it into the sea by the ton. For a long time the ocean simply swallowed it. Iron dissolved in the water soaked up the oxygen and sank as rust, laying down striped red rock that miners still dig out of the ground today. Eventually the iron ran out. The oxygen had nowhere left to go, so it began escaping into the sky. Scientists call this the Great Oxidation Event, and it happened about 2.4 billion years ago. It was a catastrophe. Most of the life that existed at the time was poisoned by the strange new gas. It was also the reason you exist, because oxygen carries enough energy to run a body as hungry and demanding as yours. So the air is not just something Earth has. It is something life made. The sky shields us in a second way that has nothing to do with breathing. About 1,800 miles under your feet, Earth's outer core is liquid iron, and it churns. That churning generates a magnetic field that reaches far out into space and deflects the stream of charged particles the sun throws at us without pause. Where the field funnels those particles down near the poles, they crash into the air and make it glow, and we call it the aurora. Mars has no such field. Its air was stripped away long ago, and what is left is thin enough to be almost nothing. Earth is not simply a good place that life happened to land on. Earth and life have been rebuilding each other for billions of years.

6.title: The Blue Planet We Named After Dirt
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Blue Planet We Named After Dirt

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Diameter about 7,918 miles
The densest planet in the solar system
Inner core: solid iron, around 5,400 C
Crust is only 3 to 43 miles thick
Plates drift at fingernail speed
Pale Blue Dot: Voyager 1, 1990

blocks.prompt: A Thin Skin on a Ball of Iron
blocks.text: Earth is about 7,900 miles from one side to the other, and almost none of it has anything to do with you. Start at the middle and work outward. The inner core is a ball of solid iron roughly seventy percent as wide as the moon, sitting at around 5,400 degrees Celsius, about as hot as the surface of the sun. It should be molten at that temperature. It is not, because the weight of the entire planet is pressing down on it and squeezing it solid. Around the inner core swirls the outer core, liquid iron and nickel, moving in slow currents that generate Earth's magnetic field. Above that sits the mantle, roughly 1,800 miles of hot rock that creeps like extremely stiff tar. And on top of all of it floats the crust: three to forty miles of cold stone. On a globe the size of an apple, the crust would be thinner than the skin. Everything you have ever known lives in that skin, and in the thin haze of gas above it. If Earth were shrunk to the size of a basketball, the atmosphere would be about as thick as a coat of paint. Every mountain, every ocean trench, every city, every creature ever born fits inside a film you could smudge with a thumb. That film is not still. The crust is cracked into enormous plates, and the slow churn of the mantle drags them around at roughly the speed your fingernails grow. Over millions of years that pace is enough to raise the Himalayas, tear oceans open, and haul old seafloor back down into the mantle to be melted and reused. This constant recycling matters more than it sounds. Plate tectonics buries carbon and returns it to the air over long cycles, which is a large part of why Earth's temperature has stayed inside a livable range for billions of years. No other planet we have found is known to do it. Venus is nearly Earth's twin in size and mass, and Venus has no plates. Its surface sits at around 465 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead. We are steadied from outside as well. The moon is unusually large for a planet our size, and its pull holds Earth's 23.4 degree tilt nearly constant. Without it, that tilt could wander widely over millions of years and drag the climate around with it. The moon is also drifting away from us, about an inch and a half every year, and its tidal grip is slowly slowing our spin. The days of the dinosaurs were roughly half an hour shorter than yours. In 1990, as Voyager 1 headed out of the solar system, it turned its camera back and photographed Earth from about 3.7 billion miles away. The planet came out as a dot less than a single pixel across, caught by chance in a stray beam of scattered sunlight. Every person who has ever lived, every war fought, every kindness done, all of it happened on that speck. None of this makes Earth fragile in the way that word usually lands. The planet is a 4.5 billion year old ball of iron and rock, and it will still be here long after we are not. The skin is what is fragile. The coat of paint we breathe, the film of water, the shallow warm band where life happens. That is the part we are changing, and it is the only part we cannot do without.

(Venus is the same size and mass but has no plates and is 465 C, suggesting tectonics helps keep Earth livable)
(it redirects concern from the planet to the biosphere; supported by the apple skin and paint layer scale work earlier)
